title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal to Target
statement:
`nums` and `target` are arrays of positive integers with equal lengths. One operation picks a contiguous, non-empty block of `nums` and either adds 1 to every element of the block or subtracts 1 from every element of it.

Find the fewest operations that turn `nums` into `target` (equal at every index) and return that count.
notes:
## Intuition

Only the signed gap `diff = target[i] - nums[i]` at each index matters: a positive gap needs that many increments covering `i`, a negative one that many decrements. Picture the gaps as bars above and below a line. One operation is a horizontal strip of height 1 over a contiguous range, and it can only help indices whose gaps point the same way.

Scan from left to right. The strips that already cover index `i - 1` can be stretched to cover `i` at no extra cost, as long as `i` needs the same direction. So only the part of `|diff|` that sticks out beyond the previous gap needs new operations. When the direction flips, or either gap is zero, nothing carries over and all of `|diff|` is new. A slower divide-and-conquer (the brute force) peels off the smallest gap of each same-signed run and splits the run at zeros; it reaches the same count.

## Approach

1. Start with `operations = 0` and `previous = 0`, an imaginary gap before index 0.
2. For each index compute `diff = target[i] - nums[i]`.
3. If `diff` and `previous` are both positive, pay only `max(0, diff - previous)`.
4. If both are negative, pay only `max(0, previous - diff)`, the extra depth.
5. Otherwise pay `|diff|` for new operations that start here.
6. Set `previous = diff`; after the scan return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

The gaps are `[1, 1, 1, 2]`. Index 0 pays 1 (`previous = 0`), so `operations = 1`. Indices 1 and 2 have the same positive gap as their left neighbour and pay 0. Index 3 rises from 1 to 2 and pays 1, so `operations = 2`: one increment over the whole array and one more on the last element.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): a single pass.
- Space: O(1): two numbers besides the input.

## Pitfalls

- Summing `|diff|` ignores that one operation fixes a whole stretch; taking the largest `|diff|` ignores sign changes.
- After a sign change nothing is reused, even when `|previous|` is bigger than `|diff|`.
- The answer can approach 10^13, so Java and C need a 64-bit `long`; compare signs directly instead of multiplying two gaps.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `diff` | signed gap `target[i] - nums[i]` at the current index |
| `previous` | the gap at the index before (0 before the first index) |
| `operations` | operations counted so far |

narration.3: Treat the gap before index 0 as zero, so the first index pays its whole gap.
narration.4: Scan the positions from left to right.
narration.5: The signed gap at i: positive needs increments, negative needs decrements.
narration.6: This gap and the previous one both need increments...
narration.7: ...so the previous increments stretch over i for free; pay only for the part that rises higher.
narration.9: ...so pay only for the extra depth below the previous gap.
narration.11: The direction changed or a gap is zero: nothing carries over, so |diff| new operations start here.
narration.13: Remember this gap for the next index.
narration.15: Every index now matches target; return the total.
